title: Shoe, logo and a wrong leaf
scenario:
A running-shoe brand wants a product image: its white sneaker, standing on a rain-wet street like the mood board, with its leaf logo on the shoe's side.

You have three files: the product photo, the logo file and the mood board. You use an image model that accepts several reference images. The exhibit shows what you have, the limits from the vendor's docs, and your first prompt with its result.
exhibit:
Files
  1. sneaker-side.jpg   (product photo, client-supplied, licensed)
  2. leaf-logo.png      (client's logo file)
  3. wet-street.jpg     (mood board photo, licensed by the studio)

Google docs, reference limits
                              Nano Banana 2.1 / 2   Nano Banana Pro
  objects (high fidelity)     up to 10        up to 6
  characters                  up to 4         up to 5
  style references            N/A             up to 3

First prompt
  "Use these images to make a cool sneaker ad."

Result
  The sneaker looks right. The street is a different street.
  The leaf on the shoe has 4 leaves instead of 3.

questions.prompt: You want the mood board to guide the look as a style reference, as well as using the shoe and the logo. Which model's limits in the exhibit cover that?

options.text: Nano Banana 2.1 / 2, because it allows more object references than Pro.
options.explanation: Its column shows N/A for style references. More object slots is not the same as a style slot.

options.text: Nano Banana Pro, because its column lists up to 3 style references.
options.explanation: Right. You need two object slots (shoe, logo) and one style slot. Pro's column covers both.

options.text: Either model, because reference limits are the same for all models.
options.explanation: The table shows they differ. Always read the limits of the exact model.

options.text: Neither, because a mood board cannot be used as a reference image.
options.explanation: Google lists style references as a supported job for Pro.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of the prompt is best?

options.text: "Take the sneaker from image 1 and place it on the street in image 3. Add the leaf logo from image 2 on the shoe's side, three leaves, as in the file. Keep the sneaker unchanged."
options.explanation: Right. It gives each image a role, describes the logo detail and says what must stay unchanged. This follows Google's templates for combining images and keeping details.

options.text: "Make the best possible sneaker ad using all three images in the most creative way you can. Surprise us with the shoe, the street and the logo, with lots of style and energy."
options.explanation: It gives no role to any image and no detail to protect. That is the same problem as the first prompt.

options.text: "Use only the third image as the base. Imagine a sneaker and a leaf logo yourself, in the same wet street, with nice light and a cool mood for the final ad."
options.explanation: This drops the product photo and the logo file, the two things that must look exact.

options.text: "Combine the images into one sneaker ad. Do not change anything in any of them, not the shoe, the logo or the street, in any way at all, even slightly."
options.explanation: If nothing can change, nothing can be combined. The prompt must say what stays and what moves.

questions.prompt: The new result still has a leaf that is a little different from the file. How do you handle it?

options.text: Send it. The logo is only small, and the client will not look that closely.
options.explanation: A changed logo is a brand error. OpenAI's docs warn that brand elements may not stay consistent across generations, so you check each result.

options.text: Compare with the logo file. If it is still off, place the logo in your design tool.
options.explanation: Right. A reference helps but does not promise an exact copy. A design tool places your exact file.

options.text: Ask the client to accept the new logo shape, because the model drew it that way.
options.explanation: The logo belongs to the client. A model error is not a reason to change it.

options.text: Add 10 more reference images of the logo and run the same prompt again.
options.explanation: More references can raise cost and may exceed the model's limits. They do not guarantee an exact copy.

questions.prompt: Next week you will run 300 variations with these three references on an OpenAI image model. What should you do first?

options.text: Nothing. Reference images cost the same as a text-only prompt.
options.explanation: Reference images are image inputs, and OpenAI bills image input tokens. They are not free.

options.text: Run one request, check what it used, then plan the batch.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's docs say to use the response's usage to measure token consumption. One test shows the real size before you commit to 300.

options.text: Delete two of the references to be safe, then run all 300.
options.explanation: That removes a part of the brief (shoe, logo or style) without any evidence it is needed.

options.text: Run all 300 at once and look at the bill afterwards, next month.
options.explanation: That risks a big cost you could have estimated with a single test.
